As observed in Figure 12b, the particle sample taken from within the chamber using Kapton tape shows a strong correlation in shape and texture to that observed on the sputtered thin film. Particles of similar attributes were observed to be scattered across the entire sample area and appear to be of similar origin (Figure 12c). Particle contaminations are known to create void regions in the surrounding area due to the shadowing effect during sputtering.145 Since these void regions act as permeation pathways, particle contamination from the sputtering chamber was identified to be a significant contributor to the poor barrier performance of the inorganic multilayer. To prevent turbulent gas flows from picking up small particles during pump-down and sputtering, chamber components were bead-blasted (Figure 14a and b), and the sputtering chamber bell jar was manually descaled (Figure 14c). The resulting thin film after initial chamber cleaning shows a significant reduction in particle contamination, as shown in the IZO/SLG sample Figure 15a. The residual defects observed on these samples mainly consisted of what appeared to be preexisting surface defects (i.e., cracks, scratches) on the SLG substrate. Although seed particles surrounding the racetrack, such as nodules and cones, contribute to growth defects, the results indicate that these contributions are minimal compared to the chamber components. The improved process was then used to prepare an IZO (100nm)/Ag (200nm)/IZO (100nm) film on a 3’’ X 3’’ Aluzine laminate (500µm) with little to no observable macro defects (Figure 15b and c). The sample was then shipped to a third-party company (Flex Pack Engineering) for WVTR evaluation at 25˚C and 40% R.H. using a MOCON testing setup. After 2 weeks of continuous testing, the WVTR appeared to stabilize at 0.0883 g/m2/day, with a slight downward trend approximating a 15% reduction in measured WVTR every 48 hours.
